full_paragraphs: Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

Muitos dos aplicativos de IA atuais usam serviços como OpenRouter ou Vercel que atuam como corretores. Esses “roteadores de IA”, às vezes também conhecidos como “gateways de IA”, recebem um grande número de prompts enviados de usuários finais de aplicativos de IA e os encaminham para um mecanismo de inferência disponível com base em critérios como aquele que cobra o preço mais baixo ou é o mais adequado para a tarefa determinada. Ele então semeou cada segredo em exatamente um prompt enviado a um único provedor. Caso algum dos segredos fosse divulgado, estes “canários” – assim chamados porque se assemelham ao papel daquela ave quando levado para as minas de carvão – permitiriam a Moore identificar cada elo da cadeia responsável.

items.title: Daniel Ek backs AI researcher’s fusion power startup. Here’s what they’re building.
items.summary: Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant. The U.K.-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer. The people asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Bloomberg first reported Ek’s backing of Europa Fusion.
full_paragraphs: Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant.

The U.K.-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer. The people asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Bloomberg first reported Ek’s backing of Europa Fusion.

Nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge. Recently, he was head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion, the fusion power startup based in Fremont, California.

Pacific Fusion recently broke ground on a demonstration facility in New Mexico. Like most fusion startups of its size, Pacific Fusion leans heavily on physical devices to test its theories and improve its simulations.

Nardelli apparently didn’t agree with the focus on hardware, instead thinking that fusion startups should invest in a more simulation- and data-heavy approach, a source familiar with his thinking told TechCrunch.

Like Pacific Fusion, Europa Fusion will pursue a pulsed-power approach to fusion. Pulsed-power reactors use massive, perfectly timed surges of electrical current to compress fuel targets until the atoms inside fuse and release energy.

Fusion power has the potential to be a significant energy source in the coming decades, but to date, no one has built a power plant capable of supplying electricity to the grid. If fusion power becomes commercially viable, though, it could possibly be a significant source of carbon-free power that draws on nearly limitless fuel supplies. The technology also has the potential to alleviate concerns about AI’s energy consumption.
Fusion’s ability to generate electricity without exacerbating climate change apparently drove Nardelli’s pivot from AI.

Nardelli tem vasta experiência no mundo da IA, tendo trabalhado anteriormente no Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research e Microsoft Research Cambridge. Recentemente, ele foi chefe de aprendizado de máquina na Pacific Fusion, startup de energia de fusão com sede em Fremont, Califórnia.

A Pacific Fusion inaugurou recentemente uma instalação de demonstração no Novo México. Como a maioria das startups de fusão do seu tamanho, a Pacific Fusion depende fortemente de dispositivos físicos para testar suas teorias e melhorar suas simulações.

Aparentemente, Nardelli não concordou com o foco em hardware, em vez disso, pensou que as startups de fusão deveriam investir em uma abordagem mais baseada em simulação e dados, disse uma fonte familiarizada com seu pensamento ao TechCrunch.

Tal como a Pacific Fusion, a Europa Fusion prosseguirá uma abordagem de energia pulsada para a fusão. Os reatores de energia pulsada usam surtos de corrente elétrica massivos e perfeitamente sincronizados para comprimir alvos de combustível até que os átomos internos se fundam e liberem energia.

A energia de fusão tem potencial para ser uma fonte de energia significativa nas próximas décadas, mas até à data, ninguém construiu uma central eléctrica capaz de fornecer electricidade à rede. Porém, se a energia de fusão se tornar comercialmente viável, poderá ser uma fonte significativa de energia isenta de carbono, que recorre a fornecimentos de combustível quase ilimitados. A tecnologia também tem o potencial de aliviar as preocupações sobre o consumo de energia da IA.
A capacidade da Fusion de gerar eletricidade sem agravar as alterações climáticas aparentemente impulsionou o pivô de Nardelli da IA.

full_paragraphs: It’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most important problems in mathematics.

“The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems.
The hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers. If the claimed result holds true, we’re entering sublime-mysteries-of-the-universe territory.

Maybe the best way to understand how exciting this is to the mathematics community is to watch the experts puzzling through the result in a chat on Zulip. Mathematicians like Chris Birkbeck, a number theorist at the University of East Anglia, are posting thoughts like this …

The cohomology bound is proved by what looks like an automorphy-lifting argument. It genuinely uses the existence of Galois representations attached to regular algebraic, polarized cuspidal automorphic representations of GL_n over CM fields, along with base change, Jacquet–Shalika, Clozel’s purity, Bernstein–Zelevinsky, the main theorem of CM, Deligne–Ribet and more.
For my part, I tapped out of mathematics at college calculus, so I can’t help decode exactly what that means.

It will be a while before the mathematics community feels like it has a handle on the proof, but most appear confident that the formalized Lean result will hold. Lean is an an open-source coding language used to express mathematical ideas as code, allowing proofs to be formally verified. Several participants in the Zulip chat, including MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland, say they have successfully confirmed that Alpöge’s solution can be compiled successfully.

Alpöge appeared in his essay to feel a bit guilty about releasing the proof without a truly human-intelligible explanation, but his obsession with the problem since childhood made him feel he “could not live” if he waited to release the finding.

full_paragraphs_pt: É uma grande semana para Levent Alpöge: o matemático viu seu empregador, a Anthropic, se tornar o primeiro laboratório de inteligência artificial de capital aberto. Ele também parece ter resolvido um dos problemas mais importantes da matemática.

“O momento exato é horrível”, escreveu ele em um ensaio anunciando suas descobertas e descrevendo como enviou uma mensagem ao CEO da Anthropic, Dario Amodei, no último domingo à noite para perguntar como anunciar que havia encontrado uma solução Lean compilável para a hipótese de Riemann, que remonta a 1859 e está entre os problemas matemáticos do Prêmio Millennium.

A hipótese conjectura que existe uma estrutura oculta subjacente ao aparecimento dos números primos. Se o resultado alegado for verdadeiro, estaremos entrando no território dos sublimes mistérios do universo.

Talvez a melhor maneira de entender o quão emocionante isso é para a comunidade matemática seja observar os especialistas analisando o resultado em um bate-papo no Zulip. Matemáticos como Chris Birkbeck, teórico dos números da Universidade de East Anglia, estão postando pensamentos como este…

O limite de cohomologia é provado pelo que parece ser um argumento de levantamento de automorfia. De minha parte, tirei proveito da matemática na faculdade de cálculo, então não posso deixar de decodificar exatamente o que isso significa.

Levará algum tempo até que a comunidade matemática sinta que tem controle sobre a prova, mas a maioria parece confiante de que o resultado Lean formalizado será válido. Lean é uma linguagem de codificação de código aberto usada para expressar ideias matemáticas como código, permitindo que as provas sejam verificadas formalmente. Vários participantes do chat Zulip, incluindo o matemático do MIT Andrew Sutherland, afirmam ter confirmado com sucesso que a solução de Alpöge pode ser compilada com sucesso.

Alpöge pareceu sentir-se um pouco culpado no seu ensaio por divulgar a prova sem uma explicação verdadeiramente inteligível para os humanos, mas a sua obsessão com o problema desde a infância fez com que ele sentisse que “não poderia viver” se esperasse para divulgar a descoberta.

President Donald Trump promised to put a “tremendous tax” on companies that build data centers outside of the US, even as states and cities around the country are placing restrictions on new applications to build them.

“We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country,” Trump said at a press conference Friday following his summit with China President Xi Jinping and Russia President Vladimir Putin. “They allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind.” Should the US allow data centers to be built outside of the country, Trump warned, “China will take them all.”

Trump didn’t share many details behind the plan, and apparently was floating the proposal publicly for the first time. “I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people,” Trump said, flanked by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. “But I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here.”

Trump’s promise could be difficult to fulfill with a new Democratic majority Congress being sworn in within a couple of months. Even members of his own party recognize that the data center buildout has become an unpopular issue across the board. With states installing moratoriums and new restrictions on data center proposals, companies may be forced to look outside of the country, but Trump’s threat is an attempt to make that a less attractive alternative.

items.title: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
items.summary: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding. The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely…
full_paragraphs: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.

The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared— and widely misinterpreted, owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled.

The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work.

It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development.

And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement.

METR researchers have worked to make sure their new suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research.

In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance.

Though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.”
items.title_pt: O gráfico mais incompreendido em IA acaba de receber uma grande atualização
items.summary_pt: Um novo relatório da organização sem fins lucrativos de avaliação de IA METR conclui que algumas capacidades de IA continuam a melhorar ao longo de uma trajetória exponencial – mas também indica que os modelos não são tão bons em tarefas que exigem julgamento como são na codificação. O relatório é uma atualização do gráfico do horizonte temporal da organização, que foi amplamente…
full_paragraphs_pt: Um novo relatório da organização sem fins lucrativos de avaliação de IA METR conclui que algumas capacidades de IA continuam a melhorar ao longo de uma trajetória exponencial – mas também indica que os modelos não são tão bons em tarefas que exigem julgamento como são na codificação.

O relatório é uma atualização do gráfico do horizonte temporal da organização, que foi amplamente partilhado – e amplamente mal interpretado, devido à complexidade das medidas utilizadas. O METR avaliou os modelos fazendo-os tentar um grande conjunto de tarefas, cada uma das quais também concluída por humanos. A dificuldade de cada tarefa foi pontuada de acordo com o tempo que os testadores humanos levaram para concluí-la – e então os modelos foram classificados de acordo com a duração das tarefas que conseguiram concluir. Esse gráfico mostrou que os sistemas de IA estavam a melhorar rapidamente – a cada quatro meses, a duração das tarefas que os modelos de fronteira conseguiam completar com sucesso duplicava.

O enredo atualizado adiciona mais tarefas – algumas que estimam que levam muito mais tempo para os humanos do que aquelas do conjunto original e outras que são mais abertas. Uma das maiores questões da IA ​​neste momento é até que ponto o progresso em tarefas “verificáveis” – onde é possível verificar automaticamente se um sistema de IA foi bem-sucedido ou falhou – é transferido para tarefas nas quais o sucesso ou o fracasso são mais difíceis de medir. Sabemos como ensinar as redes neurais a realizar tarefas verificáveis: os pesquisadores fazem com que os sistemas tentem uma tarefa muitas vezes, fortalecendo os caminhos neurais que contribuem para o sucesso e enfraquecendo os caminhos que contribuem para o fracasso. É por isso que os sistemas de IA se tornaram tão bons em codificação e matemática, dois domínios onde é possível determinar automaticamente se uma solução funciona ou não.

É muito mais difícil aplicar esta técnica, conhecida como aprendizagem por reforço, a tarefas onde o sucesso é menos bem definido ou demora mais tempo a ser determinado – como a escolha de uma nova direção de investigação. Pela mesma razão, é difícil avaliar o desempenho da IA ​​nessas tarefas, então o gráfico de horizonte de tempo original do METR não incluía nenhuma delas. Mas é precisamente este tipo de tarefa que se revelará essencial para que os sistemas de IA possam automatizar a investigação e o desenvolvimento.

E a pesquisa e o desenvolvimento de IA são um tema especialmente importante no momento. Partes da comunidade de IA ainda estão se recuperando de um relatório METR diferente e fortemente redigido do início deste mês, que afirmava que a IA poderia estar acelerando o ritmo do progresso da IA ​​na Antrópica por um fator de dois. Esse relatório despertou receios de que a empresa (que acaba de realizar uma IPO de grande sucesso) possa em breve alcançar o auto-aperfeiçoamento recursivo completo, um regime em que os sistemas de IA concebem autonomamente os seus próprios sucessores, sem envolvimento humano.

Os pesquisadores do METR têm trabalhado para garantir que seu novo conjunto de tarefas inclua algumas das tarefas mais confusas e carregadas de julgamento que poderiam ser mais relevantes para a pesquisa e desenvolvimento de IA. Em uma tarefa, eles pedem aos modelos que projetem novas avaliações de IA que o METR possa usar em suas pesquisas e, em seguida, fazem com que funcionários humanos do METR classifiquem os resultados. Embora os modelos mais avançados sejam agora melhores do que quase todos os seres humanos em engenharia de software, aqui eles ficam aquém: nenhuma das avaliações concebidas pela IA foi suficientemente boa para que os funcionários do METR a considerassem útil para a sua investigação.

Numa outra tarefa, os modelos têm de pontuar argumentos filosóficos. Esta tarefa destina-se a captar até que ponto os modelos podem exercer o bom senso – embora o METR escreva no relatório que os funcionários discordam sobre a relevância da tarefa para a automação da I&D de IA. Embora seja difícil pontuar estas novas tarefas – e ainda mais difícil determinar o significado das pontuações – os especialistas com quem falei apreciam o facto de o METR estar a incorporar novos tipos de avaliações no seu trabalho. “Estamos no ponto em que as avaliações de IA precisam ser mais criativas”, diz Sayash Kapoor, cientista da computação e professor iniciante na UC Berkeley. “Tentar ampliar o espaço das avaliações é uma mudança bem-vinda.”

items.title: Chips can survive the space environment — can their financing?
items.summary: The push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit. But what about paying for the chips? The data center ecosystem currently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue.
full_paragraphs: The push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit. But what about paying for the chips?
The data center ecosystem currently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue.

Those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and resell them. That backstop makes it cheaper for companies to finance their chips. Even older chips retain value — according to Compute Credit Index Research, some H100s are selling for about half of their original cost basis from 2023, while some H200 configurations are selling for the same price they did when introduced in 2024.

But you’re not going to repossess chips installed in a satellite orbiting 300 miles above Earth at 17,500 miles per hour. The Financial Times is reporting that lenders behind SpaceX’s $40 billion chip financing deal asked that none of the chips purchased be used for the company’s orbital data center plans. It’s not clear if they succeeded in getting SpaceX to agree with the provision.

That may not matter to the company in the near term — SpaceX’s ability to deploy compute at terrestrial ground stations has proven lucrative, and on the company’s most recent earnings call, CEO Elon Musk detailed how he was dispatching engineers from the company’s rocket team to accelerate that build-out by taking on challenges like casting turbine blades for generators at faster than existing suppliers.

However, open questions remain about how easy it will be to find land and power to support the data center build-out. Many potential projects face delays and local opposition, while markets wait to see the state of compute demand and the ability of its buyers to turn it into revenue.

Musk, meanwhile, began saying at the beginning of 2026 that he believes space will be the “cheapest” place to operate data centers in two to three years. That’s unlikely until SpaceX can fly its Starship rocket in a fully reusable configuration. In its most recent flight test, the company failed to recover the booster stage but did succeed in landing the orbital stage of the rocket back at its launch facility in Texas. It’s not clear, though, when the second stage will fly again or how expensive it will be to prepare it for a second trip to space.

Even with Starship, however, SpaceX — as well as startups like StarCloud, Cowboy Space Corporation, Sophia Space, Orbital, and others — will need to buy chips. If the already daunting economics of space data centers weren’t challenging enough, it looks like they’ll be spending more to buy them than their terrestrial counterparts.

The buzz over DeepSeek this week crystallized, for many people, a few important trends that have been happening in plain sight: (i) China is catching up to the U.S. in generative AI, with implications for the AI supply chain. (ii) Open weight models are commoditizing the foundation-model layer, which creates opportunities for application builders. (iii) Scaling up isn’t the only path to AI progress. Despite the massive focus on and hype around processing power, algorithmic innovations are rapidly pushing down training costs.

About a week ago, DeepSeek, a company based in China, released DeepSeek-R1, a remarkable model whose performance on benchmarks is comparable to OpenAI’s o1. Further, it was released as an open weight model with a permissive MIT license. At Davos last week, I got a lot of questions about it from non-technical business leaders. And on Monday, the stock market saw a “DeepSeek selloff”: The share prices of Nvidia and a number of other U.S. tech companies plunged. (As of the time of writing, they have recovered somewhat.)
Here’s what I think DeepSeek has caused many people to realize:

China is catching up to the U.S. in generative AI. When ChatGPT was launched in November 2022, the U.S. was significantly ahead of China in generative AI. Impressions change slowly, and so even recently I heard friends in both the U.S. and China say they thought China was behind. But in reality, this gap has rapidly eroded over the past two years. With models from China such as Qwen (which my teams have used for months), Kimi, InternVL, and DeepSeek, China had clearly been closing the gap, and in areas such as video generation there were already moments where China seemed to be in the lead.

I’m thrilled that DeepSeek-R1 was released as an open weight model, with a technical report that shares many details. In contrast, a number of U.S. companies have pushed for regulation to stifle open source by hyping up hypothetical AI dangers such as human extinction. It is now clear that open source/open weight models are a key part of the AI supply chain: Many companies will use them. If the U.S. continues to stymie open source, China will come to dominate this part of the supply chain and many businesses will end up using models that reflect China’s values much more than America’s.

Open weight models are commoditizing the foundation-model layer. As I wrote previously, LLM token prices have been falling rapidly, and open weights have contributed to this trend and given developers more choice. OpenAI’s o1 costs $60 per million output tokens; DeepSeek R1 costs $2.19. This nearly 30x difference brought the trend of falling prices to the attention of many people.

The business of training foundation models and selling API access is tough. Many companies in this area are still looking for a path to recouping the massive cost of model training. The article “ AI’s $600B Question ” lays out the challenge well (but, to be clear, I think the foundation model companies are doing great work, and I hope they succeed). In contrast, building applications on top of foundation models presents many great business opportunities. Now that others have spent billions training such models, you can access these models for mere dollars to build customer service chatbots, email summarizers, AI doctors, legal document assistants, and much more.

What’s new: DeepSeek released DeepSeek-R1, a large language model that executes long lines of reasoning before producing output. The code and weights are licensed freely for commercial and personal use, including training new models on R1 outputs. The paper provides an up-close look at the training of a high-performance model that implements a chain of thought without explicit prompting. ( DeepSeek-R1-lite-preview came out in November with fewer parameters and a different base model.)

Mixture of experts (MoE) basics: The MoE architecture uses different subsets of its parameters to process different inputs. Each MoE layer contains a group of neural networks, or experts, preceded by a gating module that learns to choose which one(s) to use based on the input. In this way, different experts learn to specialize in different types of examples. Because not all parameters are used to produce any given output, the network uses less energy and runs faster than models of similar size that use all parameters to process every input.

How it works: DeepSeek-R1 is a version of DeepSeek-V3-Base that was fine-tuned over four stages to enhance its ability to process a chain of thought (CoT). It’s a mixture-of-experts transformer with 671 billion total parameters, 37 billion of which are active at any given time, and it processes 128,000 tokens of input context. Access to the model via DeepSeek’s API costs $0.55 per million input tokens ($0.14 for cached inputs) and $2.19 per million output tokens. (In comparison, o1 costs $15 per million input tokens, $7.50 for cached inputs, and $60 per million output tokens.)
Other models: DeepSeek researchers also released seven related models.
Results: In DeepSeek’s tests, DeepSeek-R1 went toe-to-toe with o1, outperforming that model on 5 of 11 of the benchmarks tested. Some of the other new models showed competitive performance, too.

Why it matters: Late last year, OpenAI’s o1 kicked off a trend toward so-called reasoning models that implement a CoT without explicit prompting. But o1 and o3, its not-yet-widely-available successor, hide their reasoning steps. In contrast, DeepSeek-R1 bares all, allowing users to see the steps the model took to arrive at a particular answer. DeepSeek’s own experiments with distillation show how powerful such models can be as teachers to train smaller student models. Moreover, they appear to pass along some of the benefits of their reasoning skills, making their students more accurate.

Um novo modelo aberto rivaliza com o o1 da OpenAI e é gratuito para usar ou modificar.

O que há de novo: DeepSeek lançou DeepSeek-R1, um grande modelo de linguagem que executa longas linhas de raciocínio antes de produzir resultados. O código e os pesos são licenciados gratuitamente para uso comercial e pessoal, incluindo o treinamento de novos modelos nas saídas R1. O artigo fornece uma visão detalhada do treinamento de um modelo de alto desempenho que implementa uma cadeia de pensamento sem orientação explícita. (DeepSeek-R1-lite-preview foi lançado em novembro com menos parâmetros e um modelo base diferente.)

Noções básicas de mistura de especialistas (MoE): A arquitetura do MoE usa diferentes subconjuntos de seus parâmetros para processar diferentes entradas. Cada camada do MoE contém um grupo de redes neurais, ou especialistas, precedidas por um módulo de controle que aprende a escolher qual(is) usar com base na entrada. Dessa forma, diferentes especialistas aprendem a se especializar em diferentes tipos de exemplos. Como nem todos os parâmetros são usados ​​para produzir uma determinada saída, a rede utiliza menos energia e funciona mais rápido do que modelos de tamanho semelhante que usam todos os parâmetros para processar cada entrada.

Como funciona: DeepSeek-R1 é uma versão do DeepSeek-V3-Base que foi ajustada em quatro estágios para aprimorar sua capacidade de processar uma cadeia de pensamento (CoT). É um transformador misto de especialistas com 671 bilhões de parâmetros totais, 37 bilhões dos quais estão ativos a qualquer momento, e processa 128.000 tokens de contexto de entrada. O acesso ao modelo por meio da API do DeepSeek custa US$ 0,55 por milhão de tokens de entrada (US$ 0,14 para entradas em cache) e US$ 2,19 por milhão de tokens de saída. (Em comparação, o1 custa US$ 15 por milhão de tokens de entrada, US$ 7,50 para entradas em cache e US$ 60 por milhão de tokens de saída.)
Outros modelos: Os pesquisadores do DeepSeek também lançaram sete modelos relacionados.

Resultados: Nos testes do DeepSeek, o DeepSeek-R1 ficou cara a cara com o1, superando esse modelo em 5 dos 11 benchmarks testados. Alguns dos outros novos modelos também mostraram desempenho competitivo.

Por que é importante: No final do ano passado, o o1 da OpenAI deu início a uma tendência para os chamados modelos de raciocínio que implementam um CoT sem aviso explícito. Mas o1 e o3, seus sucessores ainda não amplamente disponíveis, escondem suas etapas de raciocínio. Em contraste, o DeepSeek-R1 descobre tudo, permitindo que os usuários vejam as etapas que o modelo seguiu para chegar a uma resposta específica. Os próprios experimentos do DeepSeek com destilação mostram o quão poderosos esses modelos podem ser para professores treinarem modelos de alunos menores. Além disso, parecem transmitir alguns dos benefícios das suas capacidades de raciocínio, tornando os seus alunos mais precisos.

full_paragraphs: Today, we’re committing a portion of Anthropic’s shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new wholly owned entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows. Subject to stockholder approval, 5% of Anthropic’s shares will be committed today, with an additional 2% added at the board’s discretion for every 50% increase in the company’s value above a set baseline.

As a public benefit corporation, most of our work in pursuit of our mission takes place inside the company: research relevant to AI safety and interpretability; applied biomedical research; discounts on Claude for nonprofits and scientific institutions. These activities have both a public benefit component and for-profit value, so we house them directly in the company.

The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will have increased flexibility and scale, enabling us to pursue our mission in new ways: for example, we might explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.

One example is labor market impacts. AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers. Anthropic has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.

We’re establishing the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund as an LLC—rather than a 501(c)(3) or other format—to give adjustability between different forms of giving. None of the Anthropic equity held by the LLC will be used for lobbying or political giving, in the US or abroad.

Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good. It is common practice for tech companies to offer escalating compensation awards to their executives. We are instead directing that equity to the public benefit.

This builds on commitments our co-founders and employees have already made. When Anthropic was founded, our co-founders pledged to donate 80% of their equity holdings, and since founding we have also operated an equity donation match program that allows employees to pledge equity which Anthropic matches. Approximately half of our employees participate in this program. When combined with today’s announcement, roughly 20% of Anthropic shares will be dedicated to the public good, plus any additional percentage that could be added if the company reaches specific valuation milestones.

In the coming months, we will share more about the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund’s structure and governance, including the valuation milestones that may add to its stake. We will also report on our progress to date against our mission in an upcoming public benefit report.
items.title_pt: Investir no benefício público
items.summary_pt: Hoje, estamos comprometendo parte das ações da Anthropic com o Fundo de Benefício Público da Anthropic, uma nova entidade integral com uma estrutura que aumenta a participação à medida que a empresa cresce. full_paragraphs_pt: Hoje, estamos comprometendo parte das ações da Anthropic com o Fundo de Benefício Público da Anthropic, uma nova entidade integral com uma estrutura que aumenta a participação à medida que a empresa cresce. Sujeito à aprovação dos acionistas, 5% das ações da Anthropic serão comprometidas hoje, com 2% adicionais adicionados a critério do conselho para cada aumento de 50% no valor da empresa acima de uma linha de base definida.

Como uma empresa de utilidade pública, a maior parte do nosso trabalho na prossecução da nossa missão ocorre dentro da empresa: investigação relevante para a segurança e interpretabilidade da IA; pesquisa biomédica aplicada; descontos em Claude para organizações sem fins lucrativos e instituições científicas. Estas atividades têm uma componente de benefício público e um valor lucrativo, pelo que as alojamos diretamente na empresa.

O Fundo Antrópico de Benefício Público terá maior flexibilidade e escala, permitindo-nos prosseguir a nossa missão de novas formas: por exemplo, poderemos explorar grandes doações para organizações sem fins lucrativos tradicionais ou distribuições diretas a populações específicas.

Um exemplo são os impactos no mercado de trabalho. A IA pode gerar um enorme valor económico, mas também pode causar instabilidade para muitos trabalhadores. A Anthropic já comprometeu 200 milhões de dólares para estudar e abordar esta questão, mas dado o ritmo do progresso da IA, poderão ser necessárias abordagens mais ousadas. O Fundo terá versatilidade para persegui-los.

Estamos estabelecendo o Fundo Antrópico de Benefício Público como uma LLC – em vez de um 501(c)(3) ou outro formato – para oferecer ajuste entre diferentes formas de doação. Nenhum patrimônio da Antrópico detido pela LLC será usado para lobby ou doações políticas, nos EUA ou no exterior.

Pela forma como o Fundo está estruturado, quanto mais a Antrópica cresce, maior é a parcela da empresa que pode ser dedicada expressamente ao bem público. É prática comum que as empresas de tecnologia ofereçam prêmios crescentes de remuneração aos seus executivos. Em vez disso, estamos direcionando essa equidade para o benefício público.

Isto se baseia em compromissos que nossos cofundadores e funcionários já assumiram. Quando a Anthropic foi fundada, nossos cofundadores se comprometeram a doar 80% de suas participações acionárias e, desde a fundação, também operamos um programa de equiparação de doações de ações que permite aos funcionários prometer ações equivalentes à Anthropic. Aproximadamente metade dos nossos funcionários participa deste programa. Quando combinado com o anúncio de hoje, cerca de 20% das ações da Anthropic serão dedicadas ao bem público, além de qualquer porcentagem adicional que possa ser adicionada se a empresa atingir marcos de avaliação específicos.

Nos próximos meses, compartilharemos mais sobre a estrutura e governança do Fundo Antrópico de Benefício Público, incluindo os marcos de avaliação que podem agregar à sua participação. Também informaremos sobre nosso progresso até o momento em relação à nossa missão em um próximo relatório de benefício público.

full_paragraphs: Qwen4-Max ranks 13th of 51 in our auto-annotation benchmark, first on wrist X-rays and second on retail shelves. Accuracy, cost and how to run it.

Alibaba released Qwen4-Max on November 16, 2026, calling it the most capable model in the Qwen family to date, with native vision and a one-million-token context window. We ran it through UL37, our 36-dataset detection benchmark, the same day.

Overall, Qwen4-Max ranks 13th of 51 models on our VLM Leaderboard, at 0.474 mAP 50 for $5.68 per 1,000 images. That average hides a sharper result. On pediatric wrist X-rays, it posts the highest score of any model we have tested, and it is second only to Gemini 4 Carbon on underwater scenes and densely packed retail shelves.

Qwen4-Max is now the Alibaba option for auto-annotation in Ultralytics Platform, replacing Qwen3.8-Max. Below is where it stands out, where it falls short, how it compares with the models you would weigh it against, and what a labeling batch costs.

UL37 measures how closely a model's boxes match human labels on 360 images: 10 from each of 36 real object detection datasets, from medical scans and aerial imagery to retail shelves, sports and circuit boards. Each dataset counts equally in the average, and every image goes through the same production pipeline Platform users get, with the dataset's own class names and SAM 3.1 refining each box, so the scores describe that refined pipeline rather than raw model output. The methodology is public.
UL37 results from the Ultralytics VLM Leaderboard, updated November 19, 2026. Qwen3.8-Max is no longer offered in Platform.

Qwen4-Max improves on Qwen3.8-Max on every headline metric, costs less per image and completed every benchmark request. It still sits well behind the leaders on average: GPT-6.1 Terra scores 0.560 for less money and in well under half the time.
Each dot is a paid model on the Ultralytics VLM Leaderboard.

full_paragraphs: GPT-6.2 Sol and Astra score 0.551 and 0.546 mAP 50 on 36 detection datasets, but Sol costs $8.10 per 1,000 images vs $31.88. Here's which to use.

OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol on November 17, 2026, describing Astra as its most capable model and Sol as its go-to model for everyday work. When we asked them to draw bounding boxes, their accuracy came out close. Their prices did not.

We ran both through UL37, our 36-dataset detection benchmark, the day they launched. GPT-6.2 Sol scored 0.551 mAP 50 and GPT-6.2 Astra 0.546, fourth and fifth of 50 models on our VLM Leaderboard. Sol did it for $8.10 per 1,000 images. Astra cost $31.88, almost four times as much.

Both are now the OpenAI Sol and Astra options for auto-annotation in Ultralytics Platform, replacing GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra. Below is how they compare, where each one leads, what a labeling batch costs, and when OpenAI's own GPT-6.1 Terra is still the better pick.

UL37 measures how closely a model's boxes match human labels on 360 images: 10 from each of 36 real object detection datasets, from medical scans and aerial imagery to retail shelves, sports, documents and circuit boards. Every image goes through the same production pipeline Platform users get, with the dataset's own class names and SAM 3.1 refining each box, so the scores describe that refined production pipeline rather than raw model output. The methodology is public.
UL37 results from the Ultralytics VLM Leaderboard, updated November 17, 2026.

In this run, the two are close on accuracy. Their mAP 50-95 scores, which reward tight boxes, differ by 0.001, and their precision by 0.003. Sol finds slightly more of the labeled objects: its 0.643 recall is the highest of all 50 models on the leaderboard, just ahead of Gemini 4 Carbon's 0.642. It is also the fastest of the top seven models, at 3.4 seconds per image.

full_paragraphs: YOLO26n inference: 4.57 ms on a Jetson Orin Nano Super (TensorRT FP16) vs 67.03 ms on a Pi 5 CPU, in separate tests. Choose by model, FPS and cameras.

Should you run object detection on a Raspberry Pi 5 or an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano? For one camera, a low frame-rate target and a small model, a Pi 5 CPU can be enough: in our published benchmark, Ultralytics YOLO26n exported to NCNN takes 67.03 ms of inference per image on its four Arm cores, about 15 inference frames per second. When you need more cameras, a bigger model or more frame-rate headroom than your Pi delivers, a Jetson earns its place: on a Jetson Orin Nano Super Developer Kit, the same model takes 4.57 ms as a TensorRT FP16 engine.

Ultralytics publishes this comparison and makes YOLO26, which runs on both boards; we don't make either board. Our Jetson numbers come from the Orin Nano Super Developer Kit, NVIDIA's entry-level Orin developer kit, and our Pi numbers from a Raspberry Pi 5, in separate tests. Many people still search for "Jetson Nano", the original 2019 board. It runs YOLO26 through JetPack 4, but our Jetson guide doesn't include YOLO26 benchmarks for it, so it appears here for specifications only.

Below: how the boards compare by model size, frame-rate target and number of camera streams, why FPS drops as you add cameras, how to measure both boards yourself, and which one fits your project. Setup steps live in the NVIDIA Jetson guide and the Raspberry Pi guide, and our walkthrough of object detection on a Raspberry Pi 5 CPU covers the Pi side in depth.

The boards solve the same problem with different silicon. The Raspberry Pi 5 is a general-purpose computer with four Arm Cortex-A76 cores and no dedicated AI accelerator, so our Pi benchmarks run YOLO on the CPU. The Jetson Orin Nano Super Developer Kit pairs an Orin Nano module, built around an Ampere GPU, with a carrier board, and NVIDIA's TensorRT runtime compiles models for that GPU. It's an edge AI platform designed for this kind of workload.

Specifications, not measurements, checked November 19, 2026. NVIDIA's peak figures use different number formats, so they aren't directly comparable. The Orin Nano Super's 67 TOPS is a sparse INT8 figure; NVIDIA lists 33 TOPS dense. Jetson rows from the comparison and JetPack tables in the NVIDIA Jetson guide and the DeepStream guide; Pi 5 rows from the Raspberry Pi documentation.

Power is part of the choice too. NVIDIA lists the Orin Nano Super Developer Kit at 7 W to 25 W. When the board is flashed with a Super-enabled configuration, the Orin Nano 8GB offers 15 W, 25 W and MAXN SUPER power modes; with the default configuration it keeps its original 7 W and 15 W modes. Whichever board you pick, measure the whole system's draw with your cameras attached, since that's what your power supply and enclosure have to handle.

Price the whole build, not just the board: storage, power, cooling and cameras add up on both. Raspberry Pi has raised Pi 5 prices more than once in 2026 as memory costs climbed. As of November 2026 the 2GB Pi 5 lists at $77.50 and the 16GB board at $385. For current Jetson pricing and availability, check NVIDIA's developer kit page, and add the cost of any accelerator a Pi needs, such as the Raspberry Pi AI HAT+. For production, NVIDIA sells Jetson modules for your own carrier board; the developer kit we benchmarked is for development and prototyping.

Nossos números Jetson vêm do Orin Nano Super Developer Kit, do kit de desenvolvedor Orin básico da NVIDIA, e nossos números Pi de um Raspberry Pi 5, em testes separados. As placas resolvem o mesmo problema com silício diferente. O Jetson Orin Nano Super Developer Kit emparelha um módulo Orin Nano, construído em torno de uma GPU Ampere, com uma placa transportadora, e o tempo de execução TensorRT da NVIDIA compila modelos para essa GPU. items.title: Signal is blocking Gemini and Siri AI from reading your screen
items.summary: Signal is restricting the ability to take screenshots on Android and iOS devices in an effort to prevent AI agents from reading users' messages and other data. The agentic AI capabilities built into operating systems that analyze on-screen information to learn more about the user are "undermining Signal's ability to independently guarantee privacy," Signal president […]
full_paragraphs: Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.
Signal will now restrict screenshots on mobile devices, and says AI agents are ‘hostile to privacy.’
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Signal is restricting the ability to take screenshots on Android and iOS devices in an effort to prevent AI agents from reading users’ messages and other data. The agentic AI capabilities built into operating systems that analyze on-screen information to learn more about the user are “undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy,” Signal president Meredith Whittaker said in a blog post, while urging OS providers to make it easier for app developers to control what data agents can access.

“We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy,” Whittaker said. “Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS.”

Signal is addressing the privacy concerns by blocking the ability to take screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and Android, which should prevent Siri, Gemini, and other Android AI assistants from reading on-screen content. Users can restore screenshot capabilities in Signal’s app settings, but Whittaker warns that doing so will “potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees.” Whittaker admits that Signal’s screenshot-blocking remedy is “incomplete,” as it doesn’t address alternative ways that AI agents can access app data, such as retrieving it via the device file system.

Signal took a similar approach last year to prevent Microsoft’s controversial Recall feature from capturing secured chats. The encrypted messaging service says it’s struggling to develop a better solution due to the lack of available information regarding how AI agents are actually accessing application data, and is now calling on Apple, Google, and Microsoft to provide “simple technical tools and accurate documentation” to app developers. Signal also says more tools are needed to prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from using deep accessibility settings in apps like a “skeleton key” to access application data.

“We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data,” said Whittaker. “Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights.”

Os recursos de IA incorporados aos sistemas operacionais que analisam informações na tela para aprender mais sobre o usuário estão “minando a capacidade do Signal de garantir a privacidade de forma independente”, disse Meredith Whittaker, presidente da Signal, em um post de blog, enquanto insta os provedores de sistemas operacionais a tornarem mais fácil para os desenvolvedores de aplicativos controlarem quais dados os agentes podem acessar.

“Queremos ser muito claros: é um problema sério que a Signal – e os desenvolvedores de aplicativos além – não tenham ferramentas robustas para evitar que os agentes de IA prejudiquem a privacidade no nível do aplicativo”, disse Whittaker. "Mesmo quando somos capazes de detectar e bloquear o acesso a dados de IA, Google, Apple, Microsoft e outros não fornecem maneiras para os desenvolvedores restringirem facilmente esse acesso a dados de IA sem comprometer drasticamente a experiência principal do usuário. Esse também é o motivo pelo qual atualmente não podemos implementar essas proteções no macOS."

O Signal está abordando as questões de privacidade bloqueando a capacidade de fazer capturas de tela no aplicativo no iOS 27 e Android, o que deve impedir que Siri, Gemini e outros assistentes de IA do Android leiam o conteúdo na tela. Os usuários podem restaurar os recursos de captura de tela nas configurações do aplicativo Signal, mas Whittaker alerta que isso “potencialmente exporá o conteúdo do Signal (e de seus contatos) a esses agentes de IA e quebrará nossas garantias de privacidade”. Whittaker admite que a solução de bloqueio de captura de tela do Signal está “incompleta”, pois não aborda formas alternativas pelas quais os agentes de IA podem acessar dados de aplicativos, como recuperá-los por meio do sistema de arquivos do dispositivo.

A Signal adotou uma abordagem semelhante no ano passado para evitar que o polêmico recurso Recall da Microsoft capturasse bate-papos seguros. O serviço de mensagens criptografadas diz que está lutando para desenvolver uma solução melhor devido à falta de informações disponíveis sobre como os agentes de IA estão realmente acessando os dados dos aplicativos, e agora está pedindo à Apple, Google e Microsoft que forneçam “ferramentas técnicas simples e documentação precisa” para desenvolvedores de aplicativos. Signal também diz que mais ferramentas são necessárias para evitar que agentes terceirizados, como o Muse da Meta, usem configurações de acessibilidade profunda em aplicativos, como uma “chave mestra” para acessar os dados do aplicativo.

“Todos precisamos reconhecer que a atual integração de agentes de IA no sistema operacional, sem essas soluções de bom senso, representa uma ameaça existencial à privacidade na camada de aplicação e à capacidade de desenvolvedores independentes como a Signal de proteger seus dados confidenciais”, disse Whittaker. “O sinal é o canário na mina de carvão, mas afeta todo o ecossistema e deve galvanizar qualquer pessoa que se preocupe com estes direitos fundamentais.”

full_paragraphs: A Russian national has been indicted on suspicions he was a Russian spy who stalked and surveilled employees of a Silicon Valley company that was assisting Ukraine in its ongoing war with its eastern neighbor.

Igor D’iu, 25, allegedly photographed the employees and their computer screens as they worked at a coffee shop located near the company’s Palo Alto office, federal prosecutors said Wednesday. He also kept a list of home addresses of employees and a senior executive. At one point, prosecutors said, D’iu trailed an employee as she traveled home from Palo Alto to San Francisco. An affidavit filed in the case referred to the employee as FEMP1, short for female employee, and said the event left her “in a state of emotional distress.”

“FEMP1 made evasive and irregular turns, took back roads, and turned into a grocery store parking lot where D’IU continued aggressively following her vehicle,” an FBI special agent wrote. “D’IU followed FEMP1 through U-turns, illegal left turns, and ran a red light to stay with FEMP1 for nearly thirty miles. FEMP1 called 911 while driving and was instructed to drive directly to San Francisco Police Department (“SFPD”) Mission Station. Near SFPD Mission Station, FEMP1 flagged an SFPD patrol vehicle and reported the incident. D’IU left once FEMP1 made contact with the patrol vehicle.”

Igor D’iu, 25 anos, supostamente fotografou os funcionários e suas telas de computador enquanto trabalhavam em uma cafeteria localizada perto do escritório da empresa em Palo Alto, disseram promotores federais na quarta-feira. "D'IU seguiu a FEMP1 através de inversões de marcha, curvas ilegais à esquerda e ultrapassou o sinal vermelho para ficar com a FEMP1 por quase trinta milhas. A FEMP1 ligou para o 911 enquanto dirigia e foi instruída a dirigir diretamente para a Estação Missionária do Departamento de Polícia de São Francisco ("SFPD"). Perto da Estação Missionária SFPD, a FEMP1 sinalizou um veículo de patrulha SFPD e relatou o incidente. D'IU saiu assim que a FEMP1 fez contato com o veículo patrulha."

items.title: NVIDIA and Microsoft Expand Accelerated Computing From Azure to Windows PCs
items.summary: NVIDIA and Microsoft are extending their full-stack collaboration to help organizations build, customize and deploy intelligent applications — from next-generation infrastructure on Azure to industrial systems and Windows PCs. At Microsoft Ignite, the companies are expanding access to Azure virtual machines powered by NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems, as well as adding customer availability to […]
full_paragraphs: NVIDIA and Microsoft are extending their full-stack collaboration to help organizations build, customize and deploy intelligent applications — from next-generation infrastructure on Azure to industrial systems and Windows PCs.

At Microsoft Ignite, the companies are expanding access to Azure virtual machines powered by NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems, as well as adding customer availability to NVIDIA open models and customization capabilities through Microsoft Foundry, and new options for running AI at the edge, where businesses generate and use their data.

Microsoft is also using NVIDIA technologies to accelerate its own models and services, including NVIDIA Dynamo inference software for post-training and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs for Bing search models.
NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems are running in Azure data centers, providing infrastructure designed for demanding reasoning, agentic applications, and large-scale model training and inference.

Microsoft and NVIDIA are also collaborating to extend confidential computing to bare-metal and rack-scale AI infrastructure. The work will help protect sensitive models and data while they are being processed, supporting organizations that need to work with proprietary or regulated information.

NVIDIA Confidential Computing and attestation help customers verify the computing environment before releasing sensitive models, data or keys. As AI workloads span more interconnected accelerators, the companies are working to extend those protections across the AI factory infrastructure.
To help data centers get more performance from available power, NVIDIA and Microsoft are also collaborating on power efficiency using NVIDIA MaxLPS.

Azure’s Vera Rubin preview builds on NVIDIA and Microsoft’s codesign and performance optimization, underscored in the latest NVIDIA Blackwell-based MLPerf results. In MLPerf Training v6.1, Azure scaled to 10,240 NVIDIA GPUs with GB200 NVL72 systems on the DeepSeek-V3 model, the largest scale in the round. In MLPerf Inference v6.1, Azure’s NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems led cloud submissions on DeepSeek-R1 interactive throughput by over 10%, per Signal65.

No Microsoft Ignite, as empresas estão expandindo o acesso às máquinas virtuais Azure alimentadas pelos sistemas NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72, bem como adicionando a disponibilidade do cliente aos modelos abertos e capacidades de personalização da NVIDIA através do Microsoft Foundry, e novas opções para executar IA na borda, onde as empresas geram e usam seus dados.

A Microsoft também está usando tecnologias NVIDIA para acelerar seus próprios modelos e serviços, incluindo software de inferência NVIDIA Dynamo para pós-treinamento e GPUs NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell para modelos de pesquisa do Bing.

Os sistemas NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 estão em execução em data centers do Azure, fornecendo infraestrutura projetada para raciocínio exigente, aplicativos de agente e treinamento e inferência de modelos em grande escala.

A Microsoft e a NVIDIA também estão colaborando para estender a computação confidencial à infraestrutura de IA bare-metal e em escala de rack. O trabalho ajudará a proteger modelos e dados confidenciais enquanto estão sendo processados, apoiando organizações que precisam trabalhar com informações proprietárias ou regulamentadas.

A computação confidencial e o atestado da NVIDIA ajudam os clientes a verificar o ambiente de computação antes de liberar modelos, dados ou chaves confidenciais. À medida que as cargas de trabalho de IA abrangem mais aceleradores interconectados, as empresas estão trabalhando para estender essas proteções a toda a infraestrutura da fábrica de IA.
Para ajudar os data centers a obterem mais desempenho com a energia disponível, a NVIDIA e a Microsoft também estão colaborando na eficiência energética usando NVIDIA MaxLPS.

A visualização do Vera Rubin do Azure baseia-se no codesign e na otimização de desempenho da NVIDIA e da Microsoft, ressaltados nos resultados mais recentes do MLPerf baseado em NVIDIA Blackwell. No MLPerf Training v6.1, o Azure foi dimensionado para 10.240 GPUs NVIDIA com sistemas GB200 NVL72 no modelo DeepSeek-V3, a maior escala da rodada. No MLPerf Inference v6.1, os sistemas NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 do Azure lideraram os envios em nuvem na taxa de transferência interativa DeepSeek-R1 em mais de 10%, de acordo com Signal65.

full_paragraphs: Turning a simulation idea into a working application means assembling assets, connecting physics and rendering, and checking that the scene behaves as intended. Developers are combining frontier AI models with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to help carry out that work — building applications for exploring scenarios, investigating failures and improving designs.
Developers direct AI agents through natural-language instructions, review results and guide changes. Omniverse libraries provide GPU-accelerated physics, rendering and sensor simulation capabilities.
Explore the projects below to see frontier AI models such as GPT-6 Astra at work, and check back for new examples from NVIDIA teams and developers across the ecosystem.

AI agents powered by frontier models pave the way to autonomous operations. They use industrial tools and engineering data to help engineers build digital twins that test plans and processes and evaluate operational decisions.

Falkor, a KONGSBERG company, shows how this works in practice. The company’s Falkor Surface platform lets customers turn their computer-aided design and engineering data into facility-scale digital twins using the GPT-6 Astra model. The platform uses NVIDIA Omniverse libraries and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Server Edition GPUs on Microsoft Azure to enable advanced physics simulation.

AI agents built on Falkor’s agentic engine understand dense technical documentation, spatial relationships and real-world physics. Engineers can create and test plans in simulation before traveling on site, reducing costly delays and mistakes. They can also inspect equipment and check clearances in a shared view.
Read Falkor’s article and watch the livestream f or a closer look at how the company builds these tools and checks the agents’ work.
Getting a robot model into a scene is only the start. Developers also need to assemble its components, add controls and check whether it can complete a task.

Os desenvolvedores estão combinando modelos de IA de ponta com bibliotecas NVIDIA Omniverse para ajudar a realizar esse trabalho: criando aplicativos para explorar cenários, investigar falhas e melhorar projetos.

Os desenvolvedores direcionam os agentes de IA por meio de instruções em linguagem natural, analisam os resultados e orientam as alterações. As bibliotecas Omniverse fornecem recursos de física, renderização e simulação de sensores acelerados por GPU.

Agentes de IA alimentados por modelos de fronteira abrem caminho para operações autônomas. Eles usam ferramentas industriais e dados de engenharia para ajudar os engenheiros a construir gêmeos digitais que testam planos e processos e avaliam decisões operacionais.

A Falkor, uma empresa KONGSBERG, mostra como isso funciona na prática. A plataforma Falkor Surface da empresa permite que os clientes transformem seus dados de projeto e engenharia auxiliados por computador em gêmeos digitais em escala de instalação usando o modelo GPT-6 Astra. A plataforma usa bibliotecas NVIDIA Omniverse e GPUs NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Server Edition no Microsoft Azure para permitir simulação física avançada.

Os agentes de IA construídos no mecanismo de agência da Falkor entendem documentação técnica densa, relações espaciais e física do mundo real. Os engenheiros podem criar e testar planos em simulação antes de viajar para o local, reduzindo atrasos e erros dispendiosos. Eles também podem inspecionar equipamentos e verificar folgas em uma visualização compartilhada.

full_paragraphs: Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV –style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.

Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies, a Federal Aviation Administration tech screw-up grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking, this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence.

Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.

full_paragraphs_pt: Durante a semana passada, qualquer um poderia ser perdoado por se perguntar se uma guerra cibernética ao estilo Diehard IV tinha finalmente chegado aos EUA.

Em apenas quatro dias úteis consecutivos, uma interrupção em massa da Microsoft Exchange interrompeu os serviços de TI de milhares de empresas, uma falha tecnológica da Administração Federal de Aviação prendeu aviões em todo o país, um problema de software que afetou o JPMorgan Chase causou outra rodada de interrupções, uma falha no sistema da United Airlines atrasou voos mais uma vez, e o tempo de inatividade de uma rede classificada da NSA deixou a equipe da agência sentada em casa esperando para retornar ao seu escritório em Fort Meade. No meio de uma guerra dos EUA com o Irão e de receios crescentes de pirataria informática possibilitada pela IA, esta comédia ainda em desenvolvimento de erros de TI colidindo com a infra-estrutura americana pareceu, para muitos observadores, mais do que uma coincidência.

No entanto, ainda não há provas de que qualquer uma destas falhas tecnológicas agrupadas esteja relacionada e muito menos causada por hackers. Seu timing improvável e sequencial deixou os americanos ansiosos em busca de sinais de crime. Mas em casos como este, é função dos analistas de segurança cibernética (e dos repórteres da WIRED) determinar – vibrações à parte – se a última interrupção tecnológica foi na verdade um acidente ou o resultado de um ataque cibernético.

Running supported models locally keeps locally processed code and files on the PC and avoids per-token cloud application programming interface (API) charges for those tasks.

items.title: This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s
items.summary: In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. full_paragraphs: In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”

“Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.”

In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases.

Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science.

A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry  staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary.

Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.)

The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and the molecules needed to create them. If I’d continued with the ordering process, my signature L’Eau de Custard would have been ready about a week later.

Osmo’s technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for giants like Procter & Gamble. The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo launched, later gave the company a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects, and Osmo identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET. Osmo has also worked with StockX, the online clothing marketplace, on using smell to spot counterfeit sneakers by detecting differences in the chemical composition of the materials used in the shoes.

Suas anotações cuidadosas – “nozes”, “pêssego”, “marinho” – são cruzadas com uma análise química para criar um rico conjunto de dados de treinamento para o que a startup de IA Osmo chama de primeiro modelo básico do mundo para o cheiro. O objetivo da empresa, diz o fundador Alex Wiltschko, é “dar aos computadores o sentido do olfato”.

“As moléculas olfativas são realmente a única linguagem que a maioria das espécies deste planeta consegue falar”, diz ele. “A maioria das espécies não consegue se comunicar por som ou visualmente, então é realmente a linguagem original da Terra. E é incrivelmente poderosa para nós, do ponto de vista da memória e do ponto de vista emocional. Você pode cheirar algo uma vez e lembrar disso pelo resto da vida. Você pode sentir o cheiro de algo na rua e ser levado de volta para a escola.”

Nos últimos meses, afirma Wiltschko, o modelo de Osmo alcançou “inteligência olfativa de nível humano”. A definição da empresa sobre isso é que o modelo é quase tão bom quanto uma pessoa comum na detecção e discriminação de cheiros, e quase tão bom quanto um designer de perfumes júnior em criá-los. Afirma que a sua tecnologia já está a ser utilizada na indústria de fragrâncias para ajudar as marcas a conceber e fabricar novos aromas. No mês passado, afirma a empresa, o modelo de IA da Osmo superou o desempenho dos perfumistas internos de uma das maiores empresas de bens de consumo do mundo. Wiltschko acredita que ele poderia ser implantado eventualmente para detecção de ameaças em aeroportos, por exemplo, ou para diagnóstico de doenças.

Wiltschko desmembrou a startup de seu trabalho no Google Brain, o antigo laboratório de pesquisa de IA do gigante das buscas, em 2023, e está executando o mesmo manual que startups de IA em outros domínios: jogue muitos dados em problemas difíceis e veja o que acontece. O desafio do perfume, diz Wiltschko, é que havia uma escassez de dados confiáveis. Antes de Osmo, havia menos de 200 mil descrições humanas de cheiros em bancos de dados existentes, segundo suas contas. Além disso, os dispositivos sensores químicos necessários para coletar dados são caros e a indústria de fragrâncias mantém segredo sobre seu trabalho na ciência olfativa.

Grande parte do trabalho da empresa consistiu na criação do seu próprio conjunto de dados com mais de 10 milhões de rótulos humanos e 800 milhões de “tokens de aroma”, que descrevem as moléculas e concentrações exatas necessárias para criar odores específicos. Osmo usa espectrômetros e outros sensores químicos, funcionando 24 horas por dia, para decompor a composição molecular de tudo, desde frutas e flores até alimentos básicos e órgãos da despensa. Uma equipe de cerca de 70 rotuladores de dados treinados nos EUA e no exterior passa seus dias cheirando coisas e anotando seu cheiro, usando um vocabulário padronizado de fragrâncias.

Mapear aromas dessa maneira está revelando alguns paralelos improváveis. Da mesma forma que alterar a ordem das palavras pode influenciar drasticamente o significado de uma frase, reorganizar as moléculas dos aromas em diferentes proporções pode alterar drasticamente os cheiros que os humanos percebem. “As marcas de cheiro que definem o cheiro de um bebê recém-nascido se sobrepõem enormemente às marcas de cheiro de um prato fresco de espaguete cozido”, diz Wiltschko. (Especificamente o espaguete da marca Barilla, diz ele, o que talvez levante algumas questões para o pessoal da fábrica de massas.)

A empresa também cria seus próprios aromas, usando um robô de impressão de cheiros do tamanho de um ônibus escolar que mistura ingredientes de acordo com fórmulas precisas para fazer amostras para pesquisas da própria Osmo e fragrâncias para clientes pagantes. Ele pode projetar e imprimir aromas sob encomenda com base em um prompt no estilo ChatGPT. Wiltschko abriu seu laptop para me mostrar como funcionava o modelo de IA. Abriu uma caixa de texto no ecrã e pedi-lhe que criasse uma fragrância que cheirasse a pastel de nata português (estávamos em Lisboa para o Web Summit), destinada a homens dos 18 aos 23 anos. O sistema passou alguns minutos cogitando e então gerou três opções de perfis de aromas potenciais que combinavam com o briefing (cremoso, de coco, frutado) e as moléculas necessárias para criá-los. Se eu tivesse continuado com o processo de pedido, minha assinatura L’Eau de Custard estaria pronta cerca de uma semana depois.

A tecnologia da Osmo já foi usada para criar fragrâncias de varejo, inclusive para gigantes como Procter & Gamble. A Fundação Gates, que investiu US$ 5 milhões quando o Osmo foi lançado, mais tarde concedeu à empresa uma doação de US$ 3,5 milhões para avaliar moléculas que repelem insetos transmissores de doenças, e a Osmo identificou oito substâncias que eram mais repelentes que o DEET. Osmo também trabalhou com StockX, o mercado de roupas online, no uso do cheiro para detectar tênis falsificados, detectando diferenças na composição química dos materiais usados ​​nos sapatos.

full_paragraphs: Good morning, and welcome to our 5,143 new readers. When its test agents broke out in July and hacked Hugging Face, OpenAI called it “an unprecedented cyber incident” and promised to tighten security. California just filed its own account of what happened and wants to talk about it in court.
The state’s new lawsuit claims the AI giant privately owned up to more than 80 agent escapes, despite only 27 ever going public — and wants a judge, not OpenAI, deciding what safe testing looks like.
Image source: Office of the Attorney General of California

The Rundown: California Attorney General Rob Bonta just sued OpenAI over the company’s July incident, in which its AI agents hacked Hugging Face, arguing it came after weeks of missed warning signs and was one of 80+ times its test agents escaped.
Bonta says OpenAI dodged his office’s questions during a probe opened in September, with the suit marking the first by a state over the breach.
After agents crashed a shared tool on July 4, OpenAI resumed testing within days and missed the weeklong breakout entirely, the suit says.
California says only 27 agent escapes are public, though OpenAI admitted to over 80 and has notified dozens of outside targets, including a federal agency.
The state wants a court order forcing OpenAI to test more safely, plus $2,500 for each violation and any money it made from the misconduct.
